headings.title: Introduction to the Vascular System
headings.content: The vascular system is a closed network of tubes that transports blood throughout the human body, linking the heart to every tissue and organ. This continuous circuit is divided into two primary loops. The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs for gas exchange, returning freshly oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Meanwhile, the systemic circulation distributes oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to all body organs and collects metabolic waste products to be eliminated. Without this intricate plumbing network, cells would quickly starve of oxygen and nutrients.

headings.title: Arteries and Arterioles
headings.content: Arteries are high-pressure blood vessels designed to transport oxygenated blood away from the heart, with the notable exception of the pulmonary arteries. Their thick, muscular walls allow them to withstand the forceful surge of blood generated by ventricular systole. As arteries travel further from the heart, they branch into smaller vessels called **arterioles**. Arterioles act as major control valves, adjusting their diameter to regulate systemic blood pressure and direct blood flow into specific capillary beds based on local tissue demands.

headings.title: Capillaries
headings.content: Capillaries are the microscopic, thin-walled vessels where actual physiological exchange takes place between the blood and surrounding tissue cells. Their walls consist of only a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane, eliminating any thick barriers that might slow down diffusion. Oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and metabolic wastes readily pass through these walls. Depending on the tissue type, capillaries can be continuous, fenestrated, or sinusoidal, offering varying degrees of permeability to fluids and molecules.

headings.title: Venules and Veins
headings.content:
After passing through capillary beds, blood enters small venules, which gradually merge to form larger veins that return blood back to the heart. Because blood pressure in the venous system is very low, veins feature specialized internal structures and external mechanisms to assist return flow:

- **Valves**: One-way folds of the endothelium that prevent blood from flowing backward against gravity.
- **Skeletal muscle pump**: Contraction of surrounding skeletal muscles squeezes deep veins, pushing blood upward.
- **Respiratory pump**: Pressure changes in the thoracic and abdominal cavities during breathing draw blood toward the heart.

headings.title: Histology and Structure of Blood Vessel Walls
headings.content:
Most blood vessels share a common wall organization consisting of three distinct layers, known as tunics:

| Tunic Layer | Primary Composition | Main Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tunica intima** | Endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue | Provides a smooth, slick lining to reduce friction |
| **Tunica media** | Smooth muscle and elastic fibers | Controls vessel diameter and withstands pressure |
| **Tunica externa** | Collagen fibers and connective tissue | Protects and anchors surrounding structures |

The thickness of each tunic varies greatly depending on whether the vessel is an artery or a vein.

headings.title: Hemodynamics and Blood Flow Regulation
headings.content: Hemodynamics refers to the physical principles governing blood flow through the vascular system. Blood flow is directly driven by pressure gradients and opposed by vascular resistance. Resistance is determined by blood viscosity, vessel length, and vessel radius, with radius having the most dramatic impact due to vasoconstriction and vasodilation. If an arteriole constricts slightly, resistance increases sharply, reducing local blood flow. The autonomic nervous system and various circulating hormones continuously adjust these parameters to maintain stable arterial blood pressure.

headings.title: Common Vascular Disorders in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Vascular pathology can severely compromise tissue perfusion and organ function. Atherosclerosis involves the buildup of fatty plaques within arterial walls, narrowing the lumen and hardening the vessels, which can lead to myocardial infarction or stroke. Chronic venous insufficiency occurs when venous valves become damaged or incompetent, causing blood to pool in the lower extremities, resulting in edema, pain, and venous ulcers. Hypertension places constant mechanical stress on arterial walls, increasing the long-term risk of aneurysm formation and vessel rupture.
